meta.name: Disability Claim Readiness Score
meta.source: The Disability Claim Readiness Kit (Ch 1-10) + Should I Apply for Disability? guide, Benefits Insider
meta.framingRule: All output describes preparation state, never predicts SSA's decision. Descriptive ('people with X are typically better prepared'), never directive ('you should file now') and never outcome language ('you qualify', 'you will be approved').

tiers.name: Strong Evidence Foundation
tiers.summary: Based on your answers, your evidence and preparation appear well-organized today. You appear to meet the basic rules, your medical record looks consistent, and you can describe your work limits in concrete terms.
tiers.caveat: This does not guarantee approval, and it does not mean a representative would have nothing to add to your case.

tiers.name: Promising but Incomplete
tiers.summary: Based on your answers, your situation may involve serious limitations, but the documentation appears incomplete. Specific gaps could slow the process or make it harder for SSA to understand your limitations.
tiers.caveat: This is one of the most common readiness states, and one of the most fixable. Most of the work to move toward the top tier can happen in 30 to 90 days.

tiers.name: Building Your Case
tiers.summary: Based on your answers, the medical condition may be real, but the documented case is not yet complete enough to stand on its own during review.
tiers.caveat: This is a snapshot of where the case is today. Cases in this range often move up over six to twelve months of consistent treatment and documentation.

tiers.name: Major Gaps to Address
tiers.summary: Based on your answers — or because one of the four basic rules appears not met — the case as it stands today faces significant barriers.
tiers.caveat: This is not the same as saying you cannot qualify. It says the information in front of you today may not yet show SSA a complete picture. For most people in this tier, the most valuable next step is a conversation with a qualified attorney or eligible non-attorney representative.

delayWarning: Filing dates affect potential benefits, and waiting can have costs — SSDI insured status can lapse (your Date Last Insured), and SSI back pay is tied to your filing date. If you are unsure about timing, ask SSA or a qualified representative before delaying.

gates.name: A Program That Fits You
gates.question: Do you have enough recent work to be insured for SSDI, or do your income and resources qualify you for SSI?
gates.closedMessage: Neither program path appears open based on your answers. Your readiness tier is capped at Major Gaps to Address until you confirm whether SSDI, SSI, or another benefit path applies.
gates.reopenMessage: Work credits may rebuild if you re-enter the workforce. SSI may apply if income and resources fall below the limits. In some cases another benefit entirely — early retirement at 62, state disability programs, employer long-term disability, or VA disability — may be a better fit.

gates.name: The Monthly Earnings Limit
gates.question: Are your countable current earnings above the SGA level for your situation?
gates.closedMessage: Earnings above Social Security's monthly limit usually stop a claim at the very first step of review, even when the medical evidence is serious. Your readiness tier is capped at Major Gaps to Address.
gates.reviewMessage: Your earnings may be above the monthly limit, but a recognized exception (impairment-related work expenses you pay yourself, an employer who pays you more than the work is worth, or a work attempt that failed because of your condition) may apply. This is exactly the kind of situation worth discussing with SSA or a qualified representative.
gates.reopenMessage: When countable earnings drop below the monthly limit, or when a recognized exception applies, this rule may no longer stand in the way.

gates.name: The 12-Month Rule
gates.question: Is your condition and the related work limitation expected to last at least 12 continuous months, or result in death?
gates.closedMessage: A condition clearly expected to resolve in under 12 months does not meet SSA's duration rule, even at its worst point. Your readiness tier is capped at Building Your Case.
gates.reopenMessage: If the condition does not resolve as expected and the work limitation continues, the duration rule may be satisfied. You do not have to wait the full 12 months to file — only the expected duration needs to be at least 12 months.

gates.name: Medical Evidence
gates.question: Do you have any objective medical evidence from an acceptable medical source?
gates.closedMessage: SSA decides claims on medical evidence. With no objective medical evidence from an acceptable medical source, your readiness tier is capped at Major Gaps to Address.
gates.reopenMessage: Establishing care with an SSA-recognized acceptable medical source — a physician, psychologist, psychiatrist, or certain advanced practice providers — can begin to build the medical record SSA needs.

sections.title: Your Age, Education & Past Work
sections.sourceChapter: Ch 6 & 7 · Past Work Inventory + Grid Check

questions.text: Where are you in the process right now?
questions.helpText: This doesn't affect your score — it helps us point your results at the right next step.

options.label: I was denied and I'm deciding what's next

questions.text: Have you worked and paid Social Security taxes for about 5 of the last 10 years?
questions.helpText: Most applicants 31 and older need 40 work credits, with 20 earned in the 10 years before their disability began — roughly 5 of the last 10 years worked. Younger workers need fewer credits. This is what makes you 'insured' for SSDI. You can check your exact credits free at ssa.gov/myaccount.

questions.text: Are your countable resources under {{ssi_resource_individual}} (single) or {{ssi_resource_couple}} (couple), with low household income?
questions.helpText: This is the test for SSI, the needs-based program. 'Resources' means things you own — cash, bank accounts, investments. Your home and one vehicle don't count. These limits have been the same since 1989.

questions.text: Have you looked at your Social Security earnings record in the last year?
questions.helpText: Your earnings record at ssa.gov/myaccount shows your work credits, your Date Last Insured, and your projected benefit. Errors are common — especially for self-employment income — and easier to fix before you file than after.

questions.text: Are you currently working for pay?
questions.helpText: Include any paid work — full-time, part-time, gig work, or self-employment.

questions.text: Are you earning more than {{sga_nonblind}} gross per month? ({{sga_blind}} if you are statutorily blind.)
questions.helpText: This is SSA's Substantial Gainful Activity (SGA) threshold — the earnings level that generally leads to denial at Step 1 of the evaluation, regardless of medical condition. 'Gross' means before taxes.

options.label: No, I earn less than that
Yes, I earn more than that

questions.text: Does any of the following apply to your work?
questions.helpText: SSA recognizes situations where earnings above the threshold don't count at full value: impairment-related work expenses you pay out of pocket, an employer who pays you more than your work is worth as a form of support (a subsidy), or a work attempt that failed because of your condition.

options.label: Yes, one of those may apply to me
I'm not sure what these mean for me

questions.text: Has your condition lasted — or does your doctor expect it to last — at least 12 continuous months?
questions.helpText: This is one of SSA's strictest rules. 'Expected to last' counts: you don't have to wait 12 months to file if your doctor expects the condition to last that long or to be terminal. Combinations of conditions can qualify together even if no single one would.

options.label: Yes — it has already lasted 12+ months
Yes — my doctor expects it to last 12+ months (or it is terminal)
I'm not sure what to expect
No — it's expected to resolve in under 12 months

questions.text: How much does your condition limit basic work activities — standing, walking, lifting, sitting, concentrating, remembering, dealing with others?
questions.helpText: SSA doesn't pay for a diagnosis. It pays for the inability to work. The question is what your condition stops you from doing, not what it's called.

options.label: It prevents me from doing the basic activities most jobs require
It significantly limits several of them

questions.text: Could you sustain full-time work — 8 hours a day, 5 days a week, week after week — even in an easier job than you've had before?
questions.helpText: SSA decides based on what you can sustain on a competitive, full-time, ongoing basis. Bad days count. The test isn't your best day — it's what you can keep doing.

options.label: No, I could not sustain that

questions.text: Has a doctor diagnosed you with a condition such as ALS, an aggressive or advanced cancer, end-stage renal disease, or early-onset Alzheimer's?
questions.helpText: SSA's Compassionate Allowances program fast-tracks about 300 conditions so severe that the diagnosis itself meets the disability standard. These claims are typically decided in weeks rather than months. The full list is at ssa.gov/compassionateallowances.

questions.text: Do you have a doctor or specialist you see regularly for your main condition?
questions.helpText: SSA gives weight to consistent records from a treating provider over time. A diagnosis from 18 months ago without follow-up is weaker than the same diagnosis with three recent visits.

options.label: I've seen someone, but not consistently
No, I don't have a current provider

questions.text: When did you last see a medical provider about your condition?
Do you have objective medical evidence of your condition — imaging, lab results, test results, or detailed clinical findings?
questions.helpText: SSA requires a 'medically determinable impairment' backed by objective evidence. A condition that hasn't been diagnosed or tested — no matter how real to you — generally can't be the basis for a claim.

questions.text: Has your condition been diagnosed by a physician, psychologist, psychiatrist, or advanced practice provider (like a nurse practitioner or physician assistant)?
questions.helpText: SSA requires the diagnosis to come from an 'acceptable medical source.' Other providers — chiropractors, therapists, counselors — can help document how your condition affects you, but generally can't establish the impairment by themselves.

options.label: Only by another type of provider

questions.text: Do you have copies of your medical records, or know exactly where to get them?
questions.helpText: You'll authorize SSA to obtain records, but having your own copies lets you confirm what's in your file — and what's missing — before you apply.

options.label: I know where to get them but don't have them
I'm not sure what records exist

questions.text: Are you following the treatment your providers have prescribed?
questions.helpText: SSA can deny a claim for failure to follow prescribed treatment without a good reason. Good reasons exist — cost, side effects, access — but they need to be documented, not assumed.

options.label: Partially — with reasons (cost, side effects, access)

questions.text: Can you describe your work limits in specific, concrete terms — like "I can stand for 10 minutes before pain forces me to sit"?
questions.helpText: Duration and frequency beat vague labels. "I can't lift much" tells SSA little. "I can't lift a gallon of milk without sharp pain" tells them exactly what they need.

options.label: Yes, in concrete terms like that
I haven't thought about it that way

questions.text: Are you keeping a symptom journal — day-by-day notes on what you can and can't do?
questions.helpText: SSA's Function Report (Form SSA-3373) asks for exactly this. Real-time notes carry more weight than reconstructed memory, and they help you stay consistent across every form and conversation.

questions.text: Do your medical records describe how your condition limits your daily functioning — not just the diagnosis?
questions.helpText: A record that says 'lumbar degenerative disc disease' establishes the impairment. A record that adds 'patient cannot sit longer than 20 minutes' establishes the limitation. SSA decides on the second kind.

options.label: Yes, my records describe my limitations
I'm not sure what my records say
No, they mostly just name the diagnosis

questions.text: Is your story consistent — does what you tell your doctors match what you do day to day and what you'd write on a form?
questions.helpText: SSA compares your statements across forms, medical records, and daily activities. Inconsistencies — even innocent ones — are one of the most common reasons evidence gets discounted.

options.label: There are real inconsistencies I'd need to explain

questions.text: Is there someone — a former employer, coworker, or family member — who has seen your limitations and could describe them?
questions.helpText: Third-party statements can't replace medical evidence, but they can corroborate your function story, especially for conditions that fluctuate.

questions.text: How old are you?
questions.helpText: Age doesn't change whether your condition is real. It changes how SSA evaluates whether you can adjust to other work. The rules shift at 50, 55, and 60.

questions.text: Are you within about 6 months of your next birthday milestone — 50, 55, or 60?
questions.helpText: Under SSA's borderline age rule, being within roughly 6 months of the next age category can sometimes be treated as already being there — if other vocational factors support it. It's not automatic; it's an argument worth knowing about.

questions.text: Could you still do any job you've held in the last 15 years, as you actually performed it?
questions.helpText: This is Step 4 of SSA's evaluation. Think about what the job actually required day to day — not the job title.

options.label: No, I couldn't do any of them now
Maybe one of them, with difficulty
Yes, I could still do at least one

questions.text: What's your highest level of education or recent training?
questions.helpText: At Step 5, SSA's medical-vocational guidelines weigh education. Less formal education and no recent training generally make it harder for SSA to point to other work you could adjust to.

options.label: High school or less, no recent training
College degree or recent skills training

questions.text: Do you have skills from past work that would transfer to a desk job or lighter work?
questions.helpText: If your skills transfer to lighter work you can still do, SSA is more likely to find other work you could adjust to. Physical, hands-on work histories often have fewer transferable skills — which, under the grids, can actually support approval.

options.label: No — my work has been mostly physical or hands-on
Yes, I have office or technical skills that transfer

questions.text: Could you list every job from the last 15 years — titles, dates, and what you actually did?
questions.helpText: SSA's work history report asks for exactly this. Descriptions of what you actually did matter more than titles — the same title can mean very different physical demands.

options.label: Yes, I could write it out today
Partially — I'd need to reconstruct some of it
No, that would take real work

questions.text: Do any of these apply to you? Check all that do — honest answers make the score useful.
questions.helpText: These are the patterns that most often complicate claims. Having one doesn't disqualify you — but knowing about it before SSA finds it is the whole point of a self-screen.

options.label: A gap of 6+ months in treatment without a documented reason
Not following prescribed treatment, without a medical or financial reason
Alcohol or drug use a doctor might connect to my condition
A previous denial, with no new evidence since
Work or earnings since my condition began that would be hard to explain

stage-denied.title: You mentioned a denial — watch the appeal clock
stage-denied.message: Appeals generally must be filed within 60 days of receiving a denial notice, and most people who are eventually approved were denied at least once first. If your denial is recent, confirming your exact deadline — with SSA or a qualified representative — may matter more than anything else in this report. Many representatives offer free consultations for exactly this situation.

stage-applied.title: While you wait — keep building the record
stage-applied.message: A pending application doesn't pause the evidence. Keep your treatment visits consistent, keep your symptom journal going, and keep copies of anything new. If SSA schedules an exam or sends forms, respond by the stated deadlines — and note every call's date and reference number.

dli-check.title: Check your Date Last Insured
dli-check.message: Your Date Last Insured (DLI) is the last day you meet the SSDI recent-work requirement. If it has passed, you can still qualify — but only by proving your disability began on or before that date. Pull your earnings record at ssa.gov/myaccount this week; it takes 10 minutes.

borderline-age.title: The borderline age rule may matter for you
borderline-age.message: You're close to an age category where SSA's rules shift. Being within roughly 6 months of 50, 55, or 60 can sometimes be treated as already being there — but it isn't automatic. This is worth discussing with SSA or a qualified representative.

cal-check.title: Ask about Compassionate Allowances
cal-check.message: Your diagnosis may be on SSA's Compassionate Allowances list — conditions so severe the diagnosis itself meets the standard, typically decided in weeks rather than months. Check ssa.gov/compassionateallowances, and if you file, say: "Please note in my file that I'm requesting a Compassionate Allowances review."

concurrent-benefits.title: You may be able to apply for both programs
concurrent-benefits.message: Both program paths appear open. If your SSDI benefit would be low and you meet SSI income and resource rules, SSA can determine whether you qualify for concurrent benefits — which generally extends what you receive and adds Medicaid alongside Medicare.
